an0599.user: Okay I'm losing it a bit. My SEO/organic is supposedly working — last 30 days I got 6.1 lakh impressions, 10,532 clicks, that's a 1.7% CTR which isn't even bad?? But I got 61 orders. SIXTY ONE. AOV ₹2,450. I've been running broad-match keywords and pouring effort into ranking. Why is all this traffic landing and then nothing happens? Is my CTR too low or what?
an0599.assistant:
Your CTR is fine — 1.7% on 6.1L impressions is a perfectly healthy click rate. Stop staring at it. The number that should scare you is the conversion rate: 10,532 clicks turned into 61 orders, that's 0.58%. For every 172 people who clicked, one bought. That's not a click problem, that's an intent problem.

Here's the mechanism. Broad-match keywords pull in everyone vaguely adjacent to your category — people researching, comparing, reading, killing time. High volume, low intent. You're optimising for traffic and getting it; the traffic just isn't in buying mode. A 0.58% conversion rate is the tell that you're filling the top of the funnel with browsers, not buyers.

The lever: tighten to high-intent terms. Pull a search-term report, kill the broad-match modifiers, layer in negative keywords for the obvious researchers ("how to", "DIY", "vs", "review"), and shift toward exact/phrase match on terms that signal purchase intent. You'll lose impressions — good, those impressions were costing you focus, not making you money.

Caveat: 61 orders is a thin base to slice by keyword, so don't over-rotate on any single term yet. Get the match types fixed, let it run 3-4 weeks, then read which intent buckets actually convert. But the direction is clear — you're buying clicks, you should be buying customers.

an0600.user: Meesho seller here, running Meta at ₹9.5L spend last 30 days. My problem is my dashboards are lying to me. Meta says ROAS 4.2, Shopify last-click says 1.5. One of them is wrong and I can't figure out which. This is post-iOS so I assume the tracking is just broken. Which number do I actually trust?
an0600.assistant:
Neither. That's the uncomfortable answer — you're refereeing two dashboards that will never agree, and you can keep refereeing forever because both are biased by design.

Meta's 4.2 is built on modelled conversions and a 7-day-click (often 1-day-view) window — it claims credit for sales it merely influenced, and post-iOS it fills the gaps with statistical modelling, which inflates. Shopify last-click gives the entire order to whoever was clicked last, usually a branded search or direct visit — so it under-credits the Meta ad that actually created the demand. Truth sits somewhere between 1.5 and 4.2. You will never reconcile them, because they're answering different questions.

So stop trying. Anchor on something neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Take total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify for the period. ₹9.5L over the real new-customer count gives you one honest number you can manage to, month over month. If blended CAC sits comfortably under your contribution per new customer, you're fine regardless of what either ROAS says.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs channels together, so it won't tell you which ad to scale — for that you'd run a geo-holdout or incrementality test. But for the "am I actually making money" question that's keeping you up, blended CAC is the number. Manage to that and ignore the two dashboards fighting.

an0601.user: Quick one — running Google Search for my eyewear brand. Why is my CTR low / efficiency dropping? Over the last 8 weeks I scaled spend from ₹5L to ₹9.4L. AOV is ₹1,900, margin around 62%. CAC went from ₹400 to ₹564 and ROAS slid from 4.8 to 3.4. I just want to know what's throttling it.
an0601.assistant:
It's not your CTR, and nothing is throttling you — you hit a ceiling and walked straight into it. Look at what you actually did: spend went ₹5L → ₹9.4L, nearly doubling. ROAS fell 4.8 → 3.4 and CAC climbed ₹400 → ₹564 over the exact same window. That's not a problem with the account; that's the predictable cost of buying more of a finite thing.

The mechanism is saturation. Google Search demand for your eyewear terms is bounded — there are only so many people typing high-intent queries this month. Your first ₹5L scooped up the cheapest, hottest intent at ₹400 a head. The next ₹4.4L had to reach colder, broader, more expensive queries, so the marginal customer costs ₹564 and the blended ROAS drops. That CAC curve bending upward as spend rises is the signature of a channel at its efficient ceiling.

Good news: you're still healthy. Contribution is ₹1,900 × 62% − ₹564 = +₹614 per order, so even the pricier customers are profitable. The lever isn't to push more budget into the same exhausted pool — it's to create new demand. New audiences, new creative angles, a second channel (Meta prospecting, Performance Max, YouTube) to feed fresh intent into Search.

Caveat: confirm it's saturation and not a seasonal dip by checking impression share — if you're already at 80%+ on your core terms, there's simply no more room there, and the answer is new demand, not a higher bid.

an0602.user: Logistics SaaS, I run WhatsApp broadcast campaigns and I think my strategy is falling apart. ROAS dropped 12% this week versus last week. I had 103 conversions this week. I'm about to tear up the whole playbook and rebuild — what's the first thing I should change??
an0602.assistant:
Change nothing. Put the playbook down.

A 12% ROAS move on 103 conversions is noise, not a trend. With a base that small, a handful of orders shifting timing — someone buying Monday instead of the previous Sunday — swings your weekly ROAS by double digits all on its own. You're reading random variance as a signal, and overhauling a strategy on one noisy week is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts into the ground: you'll change five things, next week reverts on its own, and now you can't tell which change did what.

What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band — think a 30-40%+ drop, not 12%. Until then, this is inside the envelope of normal.

So this week's job is to do nothing and let the data accumulate. Sit on your hands, keep the campaigns running as-is, and look again at a 4-week trend line. If it's still sliding then, we diagnose. Right now there's nothing to diagnose.

an0603.user: D2C apparel, last 90 days doing about ₹30L/month. Channel mix: Amazon Ads is 91% of revenue, everything else is the remaining 9%. Unit economics on Amazon are healthy. Pasting it because something feels off but I can't name it — what's wrong here?
an0603.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with the numbers — the numbers are the problem. 91% of a ₹30L/month business riding on one channel isn't a marketing metric, it's a concentration risk, and healthy unit economics make it more seductive, not safer.

Here's what the 91% actually means: Amazon controls your demand, your data, and your customer relationship. One algorithm tweak to their ad auction, one CPM spike in your category around a sale event, one account suspension over a policy flag you didn't know existed — and ₹27L of your ₹30L evaporates overnight, with no second engine to absorb the fall. You'd go from a healthy business to a crisis in a single billing cycle, and you'd have zero control over the timing.

This isn't a fix-the-funnel read. The lever is to build a genuine second channel now — while you're choosing to, with cash flow and attention to spare — rather than scrambling to stand one up the week Amazon changes the rules. Meta prospecting to your own Shopify, a WhatsApp + email list you actually own, even a basic D2C site capturing the buyers Amazon currently rents to you. Aim to get that 91% down toward 70% over the next two quarters.

Caveat: don't yank budget off Amazon to do it — it's working and paying the bills. Fund the second channel as additive insurance. The goal isn't to leave Amazon; it's to stop being a hostage to it.

an0604.user: Footwear brand, running Google Performance Max. My narrow question: how do I lower my CAC? Last 30 days — AOV ₹800, CAC ₹379, ROAS 2.1, CTR 2.1%. The CTR seems okay so I figure the issue is just that my CAC is too high and I need to optimise the ads.
an0604.assistant:
You're asking the wrong question, and lowering CAC won't save you. Let me show you why with your own numbers.

Your gross margin is 29%. So on every ₹800 order you keep ₹800 × 29% = ₹232 of gross profit before you've paid a single rupee for the customer. Then CAC takes ₹379. Contribution = ₹232 − ₹379 = −₹147 per order. You lose ₹147 every time you make a sale, and you'd lose more by scaling. The CTR at 2.1% is genuinely fine — the ads aren't broken. The disease is upstream of the ads entirely.

Do the math on your own ask: to break even at ₹379 CAC you'd need 47% gross margin. To break even at your current 29% margin you'd need CAC under ₹232 — a 39% cut, which Performance Max is not going to magically deliver. You can't ad-optimise your way out of a margin this thin; the structure won't allow it.

The lever is margin, not media. Three places to find it: COGS (renegotiate the footwear supplier, kill your worst-margin SKUs), price (₹800 AOV is low — can you bundle a 2-pair or add-on to push AOV up), or product mix (push the styles that carry more than 29%). Move margin to ~45% and the same ₹379 CAC turns profitable overnight.

Caveat: I'm working off a blended 29% — pull margin SKU-by-SKU, because if your hero product is at 40% and a few dogs are dragging the average down, the fastest fix is just cutting the dogs.

an0605.user: Coffee brand here. Running WhatsApp broadcast. Dumping my last-30 numbers: AOV ₹1,500, CAC ₹594, ROAS 2.5, CTR 1.6%, repeat customers tracked in my cohort table. My question is straightforward — how do I lower my CAC? Feels like that's what's killing me.
an0605.assistant:
CAC isn't what's killing you — and I can prove it costs you nothing to chase. Run your contribution: ₹1,500 × 24% gross margin = ₹360 of gross profit per order. CAC eats ₹594. So contribution = ₹360 − ₹594 = −₹234 per order. You bleed ₹234 on every sale. The ROAS of 2.5 looks respectable, which is exactly the trap — at a 24% margin, 2.5 ROAS is still a loss.

The mechanism: a 24% gross margin is brutally thin for a consumer brand carrying paid acquisition. At that margin, your breakeven CAC is just ₹360 — you're at ₹594, so even halving your CAC (which WhatsApp tweaks won't do) still leaves you underwater. This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume.

The lever is to fix the economics of the product, not the broadcast. Where does coffee margin hide? Pricing first — ₹1,500 AOV at 24% suggests either you're underpriced or your COGS (beans, roasting, packaging, shipping) is too high. Push for subscription (locks repeat, kills per-order acquisition cost), bundle to lift AOV, and squeeze COGS on packaging and last-mile. Get to ~45-50% margin and the same customers become profitable.

Caveat: WhatsApp broadcast to existing buyers is nearly free and should have a far better margin profile than cold paid — so check whether that ₹594 CAC is blended across channels. If broadcast-only CAC is much lower, lean into retention there while you fix the core margin.

an0606.user: Vertical SaaS for clinics, fairly new to all this. Running Google Performance Max, ₹4L spend last 30 days. My CTR is 1.4% and I'm worried it's too low — is that why my ROAS is only 1.9? AOV ₹1,500, CAC ₹806. Just want to know if my CTR is the problem.

Here's the real read. Your gross margin is 60%, so each ₹1,500 order throws off ₹1,500 × 60% = ₹900 of gross profit. CAC is ₹806. Contribution = ₹900 − ₹806 = +₹94 per customer — and that's on the FIRST order alone. Now the number that should excite you: 30% of customers repeat within 90 days. For a SaaS-ish clinic product that's a real retention engine — every one of those repeats is contribution with zero acquisition cost attached. Your true unit economics are meaningfully better than +₹94, because the LTV stacks on top.

Caveat: ₹4L is a modest spend, so confirm the 30% repeat holds as you grow and that CAC doesn't balloon past your ₹900 breakeven when you add budget. But on these numbers, the instruction is grow, not cut.

an0607.user: Jewellery brand, Google Search. Last 30 days ROAS is 3.3 which I'm pretty happy with, AOV ₹1,450, CAC ₹435. But revenue isn't really compounding the way I expected. I think my ROAS just isn't high enough — if I can push it to 4+ I'll finally grow. That's the fix, right?

Your ROAS is a red herring, and pushing it to 4 won't fix the thing that's actually broken. Your acquisition is already working: ROAS 3.3, and first-order contribution = ₹1,450 × 53% − ₹435 = ₹768 − ₹435 = +₹334 per customer. That's a strong front end. You don't have an acquisition problem.

You have a retention hole, and it's the reason revenue won't compound. Your 90-day repeat rate is 6%. Six. With 6% repeat, there is no second layer; you're refilling a bucket with no bottom, so every month's revenue is just whatever you bought that month. No wonder it's flat.

The lever is retention before more spend. Pushing ROAS to 4 just makes you slightly more efficient at filling a leaky bucket. Fix the leak first: post-purchase WhatsApp flows, a reason to come back (new collections, restock-your-gift moments, festive cycles — jewellery is gifting-heavy), and find out why nobody reorders.

Check repeat at 180 and 365 days before you panic. But even allowing for that, 6% is low enough that retention, not ROAS, is your growth lever.

an0608.user: Amazon marketplace seller, but I run YouTube ads to drive demand. Narrow question: why is my CTR low / sliding? Over the last 6 weeks my CAC went from ₹636 to ₹1,346 and ROAS dropped 3.8 to 1.8. AOV ₹2,400, margin 45%, frequency around 2.9. Same creatives and same audience the whole time. Is YouTube's algorithm just messing with me?
an0608.assistant:
It's not the algorithm and it's not your targeting — it's that you've run the same ads at the same people until they stopped looking. This is textbook creative fatigue, and your own data spells it out.

The pattern: CAC doubled ₹636 → ₹1,346 and ROAS halved 3.8 → 1.8 over six weeks, while creatives and audience stayed unchanged the whole time. The proving number is frequency 2.9 — above the ~2.5 mark where the same viewer has now seen your ad three-plus times, the novelty's gone, and the sliding CTR is them scrolling past something they've already dismissed. When the only thing that changed is how many times people have seen the ad, fatigue is the diagnosis.

And you've crossed into losing money: contribution now = ₹2,400 × 45% − ₹1,346 = ₹1,080 − ₹1,346 = −₹266 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹636 CAC you were making ₹444; today every sale costs you ₹266.

The lever is fresh creative — new angles, not a colour swap on the old hook. Different opening 3 seconds, a new problem framing, a new format (testimonial, demo, founder-to-camera). Get frequency back down by giving the algorithm new material to spread.

But the real fix is the system, not this one refresh: build a testing cadence — a couple of new concepts in rotation every 2-3 weeks — so you never ride a single winner to exhaustion again. Caveat: this read assumes the audience size held steady; if you also narrowed targeting recently, that would accelerate the same fatigue, so check both.

an0610.user: Hi, I run a nutrition brand and I'm still figuring this stuff out. I send WhatsApp broadcasts and the reach has been huge — something like 12.4 lakh impressions last month and around 14,500 clicks, which works out to about a 1.2% click rate. The traffic being there is actually the clue to what's wrong. You're getting reach in spades — 12.4L impressions, 14,525 clicks — and then it dies at the order step: 59 orders out of 14,525 clicks is a 0.41% conversion rate. That's the number to fix, and it tells a clear story.

When you blast broad and reach huge numbers but almost nobody converts, you're collecting low-intent traffic — people who clicked out of mild curiosity, not because they were ready to buy nutrition products. Broad-match keywords and wide broadcasts are designed for volume, and volume is exactly what you got; what you didn't get is intent. A 0.41% conversion rate isn't bad luck, it's the signature of an audience that was never in buying mode. The clicks aren't the win here — they're the distraction.

The lever is to narrow hard toward intent. Tighten your keywords to purchase-signal terms, add negatives to filter out the browsers and researchers, and for the WhatsApp side, segment your list so broadcasts go to people who've shown real interest (past buyers, cart adds, replied-to-a-message) rather than everyone. Trade reach for relevance — you want fewer, hotter clicks.

an0611.user: Meesho seller, ran Performance Max last 30 days, ₹18L spend, and this is post-iOS so I half expect things to be off. The trouble is my two dashboards completely disagree. Meta-side it's telling me ROAS 4.3, but when I look at Shopify on last-click it's showing 1.7. I genuinely can't tell which one is the real number to plan around.
an0611.assistant:
You're trying to pick a winner between two numbers that are both lying to you in opposite directions — and you'll never get them to agree, because they're not measuring the same thing.

The 4.3 is the platform's self-graded report card: modelled conversions, a generous 7-day-click window, credit claimed for sales it only touched. Post-iOS it fills tracking gaps with estimation, which pushes the figure up. Shopify's 1.7 on last-click does the reverse — it hands the whole order to the final click, usually a branded search or direct visit, and gives your top-of-funnel Performance Max nothing for the demand it actually created. Real performance sits between 1.7 and 4.3, and no amount of staring reconciles them.

So stop adjudicating and switch to a number neither platform can inflate: blended CAC. Total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. You spent ₹18L — divide that by the real count of new customers for the period and you get one honest acquisition cost to plan around. Compare it to your contribution per customer; if blended CAC sits comfortably under it, you're winning regardless of which ROAS you believe.

Caveat: blended CAC won't tell you which campaign or creative to scale — it's an account-level truth, not a channel-level one. For that, run a holdout or geo-test to measure real incrementality. But for the planning question — what's my actual cost to acquire — blended CAC is the figure. Manage to that and let the two dashboards argue without you.

Cost-per-customer rising in lockstep with spend is the fingerprint of a channel hitting its efficient ceiling.

The mechanism: Performance Max found your cheapest, highest-intent pockets first and converted them at ₹495. To spend the extra ₹3.5L it had to reach further out — colder audiences, looser intent, more expensive placements — so the marginal customer now costs ₹781. And here's why you can breathe: contribution = ₹1,450 × 63% − ₹781 = ₹913.5 − ₹781 = +₹132 per order. Even your most expensive scaled customer is still profitable, thanks to that fat 63% margin. The account isn't failing; it's maturing.

The lever isn't more budget into the same pool — that just pushes CAC higher toward your ₹913 breakeven. It's to create new demand: fresh creative angles, new audience signals, or a genuine second channel to feed Performance Max new intent. Caveat: check impression share on your core terms first — if you're already dominating them, the ceiling is real and confirmed, and the only way up is widening the funnel, not raising the bid.
